title: Stories of Activism
abstract:
How are activists formed? What prompts individuals to break the barrier of apathy and take 
action to fight for social change? Through field observation and one­on­one interviews with 
young climate activists in Chicago, this project attempts to answer these questions by exploring the motivations behind youth activism. Building on foundations created by existing micromobilization research, this project zooms in on individual stories and decisions, attempting to understand how young people today transition from simply caring about a cause to taking concerted action. Interviews with young activists and sympathizers were completed and analyzed through qualitative coding, and demonstrated three recurring catalysts for climate activism: education, media, and experiences with nature. The interviews also found several barriers: fear and helplessness, and the absence of personal stake or pathways to action. These findings have implications for initiatives to increase youth involvement in climate activism, suggesting that providing young people with opportunities to engage with the outdoors and educating them on the realities of human­induced environmental degradation may lead to greater participation. They also present broader implications for discussions on micro­mobilization and recruitment for activist organizations, suggesting that youth political apathy can be combated by early, targeted, multimedia and experiential education paired with clearly articulated pathways to action. Although there may not be a formula for the creation of politically engaged citizens, three ingredients ­ knowledge of the problem, a clear personal stake, and the presentation of solutions or action steps ­ may significantly increase involvement in social movements.
